Looking at his pile of unpaid bills always makes Ramesh feel uneasy. 
More often than not, Ramesh leaves his paperwork undone and sweeps 
the floor or watches TV instead, waiting until the last moment to write 
the monthly cheques. Sometimes he incurs late fees because of his 
habit of putting things off, but in many ways the emotional toll is 
worse. ‘‘The longer the bills go unpaid,’’ says Ramesh, 58, ‘‘the more my 
anxiety soars.’’

Everyone procrastinates. ‘‘It’s part of the human condition,’’ says 
Suresh Kumar, a psychology professor at Universal University. ‘‘One of 
the ways we cope is avoidance, and that’s what procrastination comes 
down to. We want to feel good at that moment. The way to do that is 
avoid the task.’’

You can procrastinate on nearly anything, even enjoyable tasks such as 
planning a vacation. ‘‘Some people procrastinate cleaning. Some people 
procrastinate by cleaning,’’ says Dr. B.V. Rao, a management professor. 
Research has shown that the top tasks people delay are cleaning, 
advancing their careers, taking care of their health, and planning their 
finances. 


666 
 
 
 
3 P a g e 
.

One big factor for them is fear of failure, of not living up to 
expectations. Arti Singh, a 57-year-old functional health coach, 
procrastinated about looking for a new job for years. That inability to 
take action only confirmed her belief that she would never do any 
better. Some people embrace procrastination, believing that they thrive 
under pressure. But researchers have debunked that notion. ‘‘I did an 
experiment several years ago, putting procrastinators under restriction 
of time,’’ says John Brown, a psychology professor. ‘‘They did worse 
than non-procrastinators, but they thought they did better. They made 
more errors. They took longer.’’

‘‘Procrastinators experience higher levels of stress, both from leaving 
things to the last minute and from their own negative and self-critical 
feelings about their procrastination,’’ says Farah Ahmed, a psychology 
lecturer. ‘‘Some of the research has shown that this stress increases 
their vulnerability for catching colds and experiencing digestion issues, 
insomnia, migraines, and muscle tension.’’

Bedtime procrastination can lead to sleep deprivation, which in turn 
can bring about obesity, heart disease and many other health issues. 
There’s one bit of good news: People tend to procrastinate less as they 
age.

For those of us in need of motivation, the best advice might be to think 
small. Next, try sending yourself signals to prompt action. For instance, 
you might put your lights on a timed dimmer switch to encourage a 
consistent bedtime. Finally, reward yourself for each step you take 
towards your goal. After you’ve gone to the gym, take a relaxing bath. 
After you’ve paid the bills, watch your favourite TV show. 


666 
 
 
 
4 P a g e

Read the following passage carefully : 
10

Introduction : Biodiversity refers to the wide variety of living 
organisms — plants, animals, and microorganisms — that exist on 
Earth. India is one of the 17 megadiverse countries in the world, with 
ecosystems ranging from the Himalayas to the coastal regions. 
Biodiversity ensures food, medicine, oxygen, soil fertility, and balance 
in the environment. However, it is under serious threat due to 
deforestation, overpopulation, industrial pollution, and climate 
change.

Methodology : This case study is based on data collected from 
government reports, field surveys, and interviews with farmers, 
students, and forest workers. Researchers focused on biodiversity in 
forests, rivers, and agricultural land to understand its importance 
and the challenges of conservation. 


666 
 
 
 
6 P a g e

Survey Examination : A survey was carried out in three states — 
Kerala, Madhya Pradesh, and Assam. Local people were asked how 
biodiversity affected their lives. Farmers reported that many crops 
were failing due to climate change. Students recognized that forests 
are essential for clean air and water. Forest workers shared that 
several species like elephants and tigers are decreasing in number. 
The survey revealed both awareness and concern among people about 
the urgent need for conservation.

Results : The findings showed that : 
• forest cover has declined in several regions. 
• endangered species are at risk of extinction. 
• communities are directly affected by reduced rainfall, poor soil 
quality, and crop loss. 
• people believe that conservation programmes and stricter laws 
are urgently required.

Implications for Interventions : To protect biodiversity, the 
government should increase afforestation programmes and create 
strict rules against illegal hunting and logging. Schools should 
promote biodiversity education to raise awareness among children. 
Farmers should be encouraged to use organic farming, water 
conservation, and mixed cropping. Non-governmental organizations 
(NGOs) and local communities must work together to restore forests, 
rivers, and wetlands.

Conclusion : Biodiversity is the foundation of human survival. It 
gives us food, medicine, water, and clean air. If biodiversity is 
destroyed, humans will also suffer. This case study highlights the 
urgent need for conservation efforts in India. Only by working 
together — governments, communities, and individuals — can we 
protect biodiversity and ensure a healthy future for generations to 
come. 
 


666 
 
 
 
7 P a g e 
.

increasingly being deployed to perform routine yet essential functions 
such as medicine delivery, room disinfection and food distribution. 
During the COVID-19 pandemic, their use in contactless service 
delivery proved invaluable in reducing exposure risks and maintaining 
stringent hygiene protocols. The advent of diagnostic robotics further 
underscores the transformative power of AI in medicine. These 
intelligent systems analyse medical data and imagery with exceptional

Introduction : Deforestation, the clearing of forest land for other 
uses, is a global environmental catastrophe with profound and often 
irreversible consequences. While its impact on climate change and 
biodiversity loss is widely recognised, its most immediate and 
devastating effects are often borne by indigenous tribes, whose 
existence is inextricably linked to the health of forest ecosystems. 
These communities, guardians of ancient knowledge and sustainable 
practices, face not only the loss of their physical homes but also the 
erosion of their cultural identity and traditional livelihoods.

Survey Examination : Consider the plight of the Arava Tribe, a 
hypothetical indigenous community living deep within a remote part 
of the Arava Basin. For generations, the Arava have co-existed

knowledge, once practical for survival, becomes less relevant in a 
deforested landscape, leading to cultural erosion, particularly among 
younger generations. This disruption often results in increased 
poverty, loss of identity and heightened conflict with encroaching 
outsiders.

Robotics is transforming the healthcare landscape by revolutionizing 
the way medical procedures are executed, patients are managed and 
hospital operations are streamlined. The seamless integration of 
artificial intelligence (AI), engineering and automation has catalysed 
the emergence of cutting-edge robotic technologies that are making 
healthcare more precise, efficient and accessible than ever before. From 
surgical theatres to outpatient clinics, robotics is enhancing workflow 
efficiency and significantly improving clinical outcomes.

Among its most notable applications is robot-assisted surgery. 
Advanced systems such as the ‘Da Vinci Surgical Robot’ empower 
surgeons with superior visualization, refined control and pinpoint 
accuracy. These minimally invasive techniques reduce surgical trauma, 
minimize complications and shorten recovery periods. Robotic surgery 
has proven especially transformative in intricate disciplines like 
cardiothoracic, gynaecological and neurosurgical procedures where 
precision is paramount.

In the realm of rehabilitation therapy, robotics play a crucial role in 
helping patients regain motor functions following strokes, spinal cord 
injuries or orthopaedic surgeries. Devices like robotic exoskeletons and 
motion-guided 
therapy 
systems 
provide

repetitive 
movements that are vital for neuro-muscular recovery — often 
surpassing the capabilities of manual therapy. These systems also 
enable real-time monitoring and adaptive treatment planning, offering 
a more individualized and effective rehabilitation process.

Hospital automation is another rapidly expanding frontier. Robots are 
increasingly being deployed to perform routine yet essential functions 
such as medicine delivery, room disinfection and food distribution. 
During the COVID-19 pandemic, their use in contactless service 
delivery proved invaluable in reducing exposure risks and maintaining 
stringent hygiene protocols. The advent of diagnostic robotics further 
underscores the transformative power of AI in medicine. These 
intelligent systems analyse medical data and imagery with exceptional 
accuracy, facilitating early detection of conditions such as cancer, 
cardio-vascular disease and diabetes. By enhancing diagnostic speed 
and reliability, they significantly contribute to timely and effective 
intervention.

In the field of geriatric care, assistive robots are being developed to 
support elderly individuals with medication reminders, vital sign 
monitoring and social engagement. These robots offer not only physical 
assistance but also emotional support, helping combat loneliness and 
cognitive decline — especially for those living alone or with limited 
human interaction.

While the integration of robotics into healthcare does pose challenges 
— such as substantial implementation costs, the need for specialized 
training and concerns about diminished human connection — the 
long-term advantages far outweigh these limitations.

As healthcare systems worldwide strive for greater accuracy, efficiency 
and inclusivity, robotics stands out as a catalyst for innovation. Its 
expanding role — from surgical precision to hospital automation and 
personalized patient care — heralds a future where technology and 
empathy coalesce to create a more advanced and humane healthcare 
ecosystem.

Introduction : Deforestation, the clearing of forest land for other 
uses, is a global environmental catastrophe with profound and often 
irreversible consequences. While its impact on climate change and 
biodiversity loss is widely recognised, its most immediate and 
devastating effects are often borne by indigenous tribes, whose 
existence is inextricably linked to the health of forest ecosystems. 
These communities, guardians of ancient knowledge and sustainable 
practices, face not only the loss of their physical homes but also the 
erosion of their cultural identity and traditional livelihoods.

Survey Examination : Consider the plight of the Arava Tribe, a 
hypothetical indigenous community living deep within a remote part 
of the Arava Basin. For generations, the Arava have co-existed 
peacefully with the rainforest, drawing from its richness for food, 
healing and spiritual nourishment. Their traditional knowledge, 
passed 
down 
through 
generations, 
encompasses 
intricate 
understanding of plant properties, animal behaviour and sustainable 
resource management. The Arava’s diet comprises forest-sourced 
fruits, nuts, wild game and freshwater fish, reflecting their deep 
ecological integration. Their shelters, constructed from indigenous 
materials and their ceremonial practices, aligned with seasonal forest 
rhythms, underscore a lifestyle symbiotically tied to their natural 
surroundings. 


666 
 
 
6 P a g e

Methodology and Implications : Moreover, in recent decades, the 
Arava’s ancestral lands have been encroached upon by illegal logging 
operations, cattle ranching and agricultural expansion. Vast tracts of 
their forest homes have been systematically cleared, leading to a 
cascade of environmental and social impacts. Environmentally, the 
loss of tree cover has resulted in localized climate shifts, including 
increased temperatures and altered rainfall patterns, leading to 
prolonged droughts and unpredictable floods. Biodiversity has 
plummeted, with many plant species vital for Arava medicine 
disappearing and traditional hunting grounds shrinking, impacting 
their food security. The pollution of waterways from agricultural 
runoff further compromises their health and access to clean drinking 
water.

Effects and Conclusion : From a social and cultural perspective, 
the effects are equally dire. The destruction of sacred sites within the 
forest has severed spiritual ties. The forced displacement of families 
due to land loss has led to the breakdown of community structures 
and increased vulnerability to external diseases. Traditional 
knowledge, once practical for survival, becomes less relevant in a 
deforested landscape, leading to cultural erosion, particularly among 
younger generations. This disruption often results in increased 
poverty, loss of identity and heightened conflict with encroaching 
outsiders.

Jonathan Seagull discovered that boredom, fear and anger are the 
reasons a gull’s life is so short and with those gone from his thought, 
he lived a long, fine life indeed.

They laughed at him. The other gulls scorned him. ‘Such nonsense’, 
they would squawk, as he practised flying, not for food but for the joy 
of flight itself. But Jonathan, undeterred, flew higher and faster than 
any gull before him. He learned that the secret to flight was not 
merely flapping wings, but in knowing the purpose of flying.

‘Break the chain of your thought’, he told himself, ‘And you break the 
chains of your body.’ 
 
 
In solitude, he mastered loops, dives and rolls. He flew at speeds that 
blurred the ocean below. The flock cast him out for defying tradition, 
he discovered that exile was not the end but a beginning. Alone, he 
found peace. Alone, he found the sky. 


 
 
 
3 P a g e 
 
.

One morning, soaring silently above the clouds, Jonathan was joined 
by two radiant gulls. Their wings shone with light and their presence 
was calm and sure. ‘We’ve been watching you’, they said. ‘You’re 
ready to come with us.’ 
 
 
‘Where ?’ Jonathan asked blinking in the sunlight. 
 
 
‘To a higher level of being,’ they answered. 
 
 
‘You have learned much but there is more – more to flying, more to 
being a gull.’

He followed them into a realm where flight was pure thought and 
time had no meaning. There, gulls didn’t fight over scraps of bread or 
squawk at one another in fear. They flew to understand themselves 
to explore the limitless. There Jonathan met Chiang, the wisest gull, 
who told him : ‘The only true law is that which leads to freedom – 
there is no other.’

Jonathan began to teach others what he had learned, sharing not 
just flight techniques but freedom of thought. ‘You can go as far as 
you wish,’ he would say. ‘Because you have the right to learn. You 
have the right to be free.’ 
 
 
No longer bound by rules, written in sand, Jonathan soared not just 
through the skies but through understanding. And as he flew, he 
knew that greatness is not measured in a wingspan but in the 
courage to break free. (365 words) 
 
 
Source : Jonathan Livingstone Seagull by Richard Bach.

being a gull.’

He followed them into a realm where flight was pure thought and 
time had no meaning. There, gulls didn’t fight over scraps of bread or 
squawk at one another in fear. They flew to understand themselves 
to explore the limitless. There Jonathan met Chiang, the wisest gull, 
who told him : ‘The only true law is that which leads to freedom – 
there is no other.’

Jonathan began to teach others what he had learned, sharing not 
just flight techniques but freedom of thought. ‘You can go as far as 
you wish,’ he would say. ‘Because you have the right to learn. You 
have the right to be free.’ 
 
 
No longer bound by rules, written in sand, Jonathan soared not just 
through the skies but through understanding. And as he flew, he 
knew that greatness is not measured in a wingspan but in the 
courage to break free. (365 words)

Chronobiology : The Science of Time is within Us.

Beneath the conscious rhythm of our waking lives lies a subtler, 
deeply embedded tempo of our body’s internal clock, orchestrated by 
the field of chronobiology. This clock doesn’t tick with mechanical 
precision but rather responds to cues from nature: the rising sun, the 
fading light, or the temperature of the wind. Governed by the 
suprachiasmatic nucleus in the brain, this circadian rhythm aligns 
our sleep, metabolism, hormone release, and even mood with the 24-
hour cycle.

Scientists have discovered that disrupting this internal clock 
whether through jet lag, night shifts, or excessive exposure to 
screens can lead to a biological desynchronization that affects 
everything from digestion to memory. A study from the University of 
Colorado found that just one week of camping away from artificial 
light, resets participants’ circadian rhythm entirely. The body, it 
seems, remembers the sun even when the mind forgets.

What’s striking is the clock’s inflexible loyalty to nature. Artificial 
attempts to override it such as caffeine-induced wakefulness or 
screen-induced sleeplessness may work temporarily but often has a 
hidden cost : chronic fatigue, hormonal imbalance, and weakened 
immunity. Its not just sleep we lose, it’s the invisible equilibrium 
that our biology depends on. 


 
 
 
4 P a g e

Modern life, with its blurring of day and night, has birthed what 
experts call ‘social jet lag’ a state where our societal obligations pull 
us in one temporal direction, while our biology tugs us in another. 
Adolescents are particularly vulnerable, as their natural clocks shift 
later during puberty, clashing with early school timings. The result ? 
A generation persistently deprived of meaningful rest.

What is the way forward – we need to understand that sleep 
deficiency and chronic fatigue are considered major risk factors for 
diseases, depression, and accidents. People must take care of sleep 
hygiene at regular time, avoid screen time before bed time, and 
ensure comfortable conditions. Taking short breaks for stretching, 
breathing, or a few hours of exercise reduces tension. When body 
demands rest, it should not be ignored. One must respond to it 
rather than ignoring it.

Chronobiologists argue that respecting internal time could transform 
public health. Adjusting school hours, designing light-conscious 
architecture or aligning work shifts with biological peaks could 
reduce stress and enhance productivity. As we continue racing 
against time, perhaps the most radical act is to slow down and listen 
to the timekeepers within us quiet, persistent and wise.

Beneath the conscious rhythm of our waking lives lies a subtler, 
deeply embedded tempo of our body’s internal clock, orchestrated by 
the field of chronobiology. This clock doesn’t tick with mechanical 
precision but rather responds to cues from nature : the rising sun,

our sleep, metabolism, hormone release, and even mood with the 24-

whether through jet lag, night shifts, or excessive exposure to 
screens can lead to a biological desynchronization that affects 
everything from digestion to memory. A study from the University of 
Colorado found that just one week of camping away from artificial 
light, resets participants’ circadian rhythm entirely. The body, it 
seems, remembers the sun even when the mind forgets.

What’s striking is the clock’s inflexible loyalty to nature. Artificial 
attempts to override it such as caffeine-induced wakefulness or 
screen-induced sleeplessness may work temporarily but often has a 
hidden cost : chronic fatigue, hormonal imbalance and weakened 
immunity. Its not just sleep we lose, it’s the invisible equilibrium 
that our biology depends on.

experts call ‘social jet lag’ a state where our societal obligations pull 
us in one temporal direction, while our biology tugs us in another.

later during puberty, clashing with early school timings. The result ? 
A generation persistently deprived of meaningful rest.

deficiency and chronic fatigue are considered major risk factors for 
diseases, depression and accidents. People must take care of sleep 
hygiene at regular time, avoid screen time before bed time, and 
ensure comfortable conditions. Taking short breaks for stretching, 
breathing, or a few hours of exercise reduces tension. When body 
demands rest, it should not be ignored. One must respond to it 
rather than ignoring it.

public health. Adjusting school hours, designing light-conscious 
architecture or aligning work shifts with biological peaks could 
reduce stress and enhance productivity. As we continue racing 
against time, perhaps the most radical act is to slow down and listen 
to the timekeepers within us quiet, persistent and wise.

Almost everyone engages with social media in some form. Whether it 
is updating a status, sharing photos of a family gathering, or scrolling 
through friends’ vacation highlights, it is inevitable that most 
individuals use online social platforms.

People tend to view social media as synonymous with shallow 
interactions, digital obsession, or the carefully curated presentation of 
an idealised life. But researchers often define it as ‘‘an extension of 
human social connection’’, says a professor of digital anthropology. 
‘‘It is something that fulfils the fundamental human need for 
belonging’’ as it is an integral part of modern communication, 
relationship maintenance and even identity formation.

‘‘It is not inherently harmful’’, adds a social psychologist. ‘‘It can be 
positive or neutral.’’ Some researchers argue that social media helped 
us adapt to an increasingly mobile world. Digital sociologists 
pioneered this perspective, comparing social media usage to the 
community gatherings our ancestors valued as a means of 
maintaining social bonds.

People are usually resistant to thinking about social media as 
anything but problematic. It is true that there are some types of 
engagement that should be avoided, such as social media use that 
fosters unhealthy comparisons or contributes to a poor self-image. In 
such scenarios, no one benefits. Social media engagement can also be 
both active and passive. Active engagement refers to directly creating 
and sharing content, commenting on others’ posts or initiating online 
conversations. An active user contributes original material and drives 
discussions. Passive consumption, on the other hand, involves more 
observational behaviour like scrolling without interacting, watching 
without commenting or reading updates without acknowledging them, 
while still allowing content algorithms to shape one’s feed through 
these subtle interactions. 


 
 
 
 3 
.

It is interesting to note that social media usage also reveals 
something about the relationships people have with themselves and 
others. The type of content someone shares often reflects their values 
and self-perception, which are key aspects of personal identity.

Research has found that mindful social media use can enhance 
connection, while other studies have found it can serve as a platform 
for self-expression and creativity. So, approach your feed thoughtfully, 
remembering that some benefit can come from it when used with the 
right intentions.

Almost everyone engages with social media in some form. Whether it 
is updating a status, sharing photos of a family gathering, or scrolling 
through friends’ vacation highlights, it is inevitable that most 
individuals use online social platforms.

People tend to view social media as synonymous with shallow 
interactions, digital obsession, or the carefully curated presentation of 
an idealised life. But researchers often define it as ‘‘an extension of 
human social connection’’, says a professor of digital anthropology. 
‘‘It is something that fulfils the fundamental human need for 
belonging’’ as it is an integral part of modern communication, 
relationship maintenance and even identity formation.

‘‘It is not inherently harmful’’, adds a social psychologist. ‘‘It can be 
positive or neutral.’’ Some researchers argue that social media helped 
us adapt to an increasingly mobile world. Digital sociologists 
pioneered this perspective, comparing social media usage to the 
community gatherings our ancestors valued as a means of 
maintaining social bonds.

People are usually resistant to thinking about social media as 
anything but problematic. It is true that there are some types of 
engagement that should be avoided, such as social media use that 
fosters unhealthy comparisons or contributes to a poor self-image. In 
such scenarios, no one benefits. Social media engagement can also be 
both active and passive. Active engagement refers to directly creating 
and sharing content, commenting on others’ posts or initiating online 
conversations. An active user contributes original material and drives 
discussions. Passive consumption, on the other hand, involves more 
observational behaviour like scrolling without interacting, watching 
without commenting or reading updates without acknowledging them, 
while still allowing content algorithms to shape one’s feed through 
these subtle interactions. 


 
 
 
 3 
.

It is interesting to note that social media usage also reveals 
something about the relationships people have with themselves and 
others. The type of content someone shares often reflects their values 
and self-perception, which are key aspects of personal identity.

Research has found that mindful social media use can enhance 
connection, while other studies have found it can serve as a platform 
for self-expression and creativity. So, approach your feed thoughtfully, 
remembering that some benefit can come from it when used with the 
right intentions.

Introduction : 
 
Students constantly seek methods to enhance their learning 
experience and academic performance. This research shows that 
music has long been considered a potential factor in creating 
productive study environments. It examines the influence of different 
music genres, including classical Indian music, on students’ 
concentration, retention, and overall study effectiveness. The current 
investigation provides insights into how various musical elements 
impact cognitive functions during study sessions among secondary 
school students. The study is relevant in the present times as digital 
influences govern our lives to quite an extent and pose a distraction. 


 
 
 
 5 
.

A structured questionnaire along with controlled study sessions was 
employed to gather information on the subject. Participants were

and 
memory 
tasks 
to 
measure 
performance 
objectively.

appeared to stimulate neutral pathways associated with logical

distraction by activating language processing centres. The tempo and

study 
environment.

would 
benefit 
from 
experimenting with different music conditions to determine what 
works best for their individual cognitive styles rather than simply 
choosing based on their personal preferences.
